projects.title: Email-to-Call Intake Automation
projects.summary: An intake workflow connecting inbound email to firm-specific routing, scheduled AI calling, and CasePeer. The engineering work sits between the message arriving and the resulting interaction becoming useful to the receiving team.
projects.challenge: Email intake, phone contact, scheduling, and case management have different data shapes and execution timelines. Joining them requires more than a synchronous chain of API calls: the workflow must preserve routing context and retain scheduled work beyond the lifetime of the inbound request.
approach: Receive email events through Resend and use a signed webhook as the intake boundary.
Route the intake to the appropriate firm and extract phone information for the next stage of processing.
Use durable scheduled work to coordinate AI calling through ElevenLabs and Twilio rather than relying on an in-process timer.
Connect the calling workflow to CasePeer so intake information and follow-up can reach the case-management workflow.
projects.outcome: A connected intake workflow that carries firm-specific context from inbound email through scheduled AI calling to CasePeer, bringing intake processing and case-management follow-up into the same integration path.

projects.title: BMail — Business Email Service
projects.summary: I built BMail after recurring email blocks exposed a need for better control over business communication. The internal release combines team access, approved sender identities, attachments, queued sending, and audit history—a working foundation for a broader business email service, starting with outbound communication.
projects.challenge: Email reliability was an operational problem with a product gap behind it. Shared sending reputation, domain-authentication configuration, mailbox routing, and sender verification could each affect a message's journey. The team needed a clear way to compose and submit messages, use approved identities, and understand what had happened without managing SMTP credentials or interpreting server logs.
approach: Build the team experience: individual logins, administrator-managed access, approved sender identities, a composer with To/CC/BCC, attachments, and editable starter templates. Enforce a sender copy in CC on the backend so correspondence also reaches the user's existing mailbox.

Design the application around explicit workflow state: a persistent sending queue, duplicate-submit protection, personal history, and an audit trail. Distinguish relay acceptance, partial rejection, failure, and uncertain completion so a connection interruption does not trigger an unsafe automatic resend.

Keep the initial service lightweight: use Flask and server-rendered templates with one background worker, SQLCipher-encrypted SQLite storage, and server-side SMTP credentials. Add sender authorization, CSRF protection, password hashing, and sending limits around the workflow.

Connect product and mail operations: integrate authenticated SMTP over verified STARTTLS, work through SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment and same-domain routing issues, and preserve existing mailboxes for incoming messages and replies.

Deliver the application as a Docker deployment with persistent data and HTTPS access through Cloudflare Tunnel. Migrate existing accounts and message history, then verify the browser experience and SMTP connectivity.
projects.outcome: A deployed internal service that gives the team an application for controlled business-email sending, rather than requiring direct access to mail-server configuration. The current setup uses infrastructure under the team's control and avoids an additional email-platform software subscription, while hosting and operations remain part of running the service.
flow: Team login and approved sender selection
Submission status, history, and audit trail

builderStory.origin: I started building BMail because recurring outgoing-email blocks were interrupting the team's communication. Fixing the transport was only the first step: people still needed a simple interface, clear permissions, and useful feedback. I turned that operational problem into a lightweight product that the team could use, with a foundation for a more complete business email service.
lessons: Infrastructure becomes a service when people can use it without understanding the servers underneath. Account management, sender permissions, composition, and history were product requirements, not finishing touches.

A successful SMTP submission is not the same as arrival in a recipient's inbox. Authentication, routing, sender verification, and later bounces are distinct concerns, so the interface must describe the status it actually knows.

The smallest useful release made the product practical to operate. A lightweight application and encrypted local storage supported the internal workflow without introducing a separate frontend build, external database, or queue service.
roadmap: Receiving and conversation workflows: explore inbound processing, reply threading, and shared-inbox capabilities to bring sending and receiving into one team workspace.
Domain and team onboarding: develop guided domain verification, sender provisioning, and organization-level access boundaries for a reusable service beyond the initial team.
Delivery feedback: integrate bounce and delivery-event processing, actionable diagnostics, and administrative reporting beyond the current submission-status view.
Application integrations: add a developer-facing API, reusable templates, and event-driven transactional messaging for business applications.
Service operations: extend retention controls, tested backup and recovery procedures, observability, and capacity planning as usage grows.

faqs.question: What kind of engineering work do you focus on?
faqs.answer: I focus on AI automation, payments, full-stack SaaS, and cloud delivery. I am particularly interested in systems where several services must cooperate reliably, such as turning inbound events into scheduled work or connecting a payment channel to an accounting workflow.

faqs.question: How much industry experience do you bring?
faqs.answer: I bring roughly ten years of industry experience across backend systems, full-stack applications, integrations, and infrastructure. That breadth helps me evaluate tradeoffs across the whole product rather than treating the interface, services, and deployment as separate problems.

faqs.question: How do you approach AI features?
faqs.answer: I treat the model or voice provider as one component of a larger system. The surrounding workflow needs clear inputs, durable state, controlled side effects, and a way for people to review uncertain or sensitive decisions. A convincing demo is a starting point, not the reliability model.

faqs.question: Do you work across frontend, backend, and infrastructure?
faqs.answer: Yes. My work spans product interfaces, APIs, integrations, and deployment. I prefer to follow the problem across those boundaries while keeping the implementation understandable for the team that will operate and extend it.
